questions.stem: Which factor contributes most to the energy in a collision?

options.text: The mass of the vehicle
options.rationale: Mass contributes linearly; speed contributes far more.

options.text: The speed
options.rationale: Correct. Doubling speed multiplies energy roughly fourfold.

options.text: The colour of the vehicle
options.rationale: Not a factor in energy transfer.

options.text: The number of occupants
options.rationale: Not the dominant determinant.

questions.stem: What are the three collisions in a vehicle crash?

options.text: Front, side and rear impact
options.rationale: Those are impact directions, not the three collisions.

options.text: Vehicle into object, occupant into vehicle, organs into the body's interior
options.rationale: Correct. The third is the one nobody pictures.

options.text: Driver, passenger and pedestrian
options.rationale: Not the model described.

options.text: Impact, rollover and ejection
options.rationale: Those are crash types, not the collision sequence.

questions.stem: A stab wound is one centimetre across. What does that tell you about internal damage?

options.text: The damage is proportionally small
options.rationale: Wound size correlates poorly with internal damage.

options.text: Very little — the damage follows the path of the blade, not the size of the hole
options.rationale: Correct. A small hole can conceal multiple organ injuries.

options.text: There is no internal damage
options.rationale: A small wound excludes nothing.

options.text: Damage is limited to the skin
options.rationale: Penetrating injury by definition goes deeper.

questions.stem: Why should you look at the vehicle before it is towed?

options.text: To assess repair costs for documentation
options.rationale: Not a clinical consideration.

options.text: Because deformation shows where the energy went, and the information is unavailable later
options.rationale: Correct. A starred windscreen and a bent wheel change what the hospital looks for.

options.text: To determine who was at fault
options.rationale: Not an EMT function.

options.text: To decide whether the patient is telling the truth
options.rationale: Not the purpose.

questions.stem: How does blunt trauma typically present externally?

options.text: With extensive open wounds
options.rationale: Open wounds are more characteristic of penetrating trauma.

options.text: Often with little to see, despite significant internal injury
options.rationale: Correct. The energy spreads and goes through.

options.text: Always with obvious deformity
options.rationale: Deformity may be entirely absent.

options.text: With bleeding that is easy to quantify
options.rationale: Blunt trauma bleeding is often internal and unquantifiable.

questions.stem: What is the correct role of mechanism in your assessment?

options.text: It determines the injuries the patient has
options.rationale: It informs, but does not determine.

options.text: It raises or lowers your index of suspicion without replacing assessment
options.rationale: Correct. It decides how hard you look, not what you find.

options.text: It replaces the physical examination in obvious cases
options.rationale: It never replaces assessment.

options.text: It is irrelevant once the patient is assessed
options.rationale: It shapes how thoroughly you assess.

questions.stem: Which of these raises the index of suspicion sharply?

options.text: The patient being anxious
options.rationale: Anxiety is not a mechanism.

options.text: Death of another occupant in the same vehicle
options.rationale: Correct. It indicates the energy available in that crash.

options.text: The vehicle being an older model
options.rationale: Not a recognised criterion.

options.text: The patient not wearing a coat
options.rationale: Not relevant to mechanism.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old falls from standing height. How significant is this mechanism?

options.text: Insignificant, since the distance was small
options.rationale: Ground-level falls are a leading cause of serious injury in older patients.

options.text: Significant — older patients are injured by considerably less energy
options.rationale: Correct. Brittle bones and reduced reserve change the meaning of the fall.

options.text: Significant only if they lost consciousness
options.rationale: Loss of consciousness is not required.

options.text: Equivalent to the same fall in a 25-year-old
options.rationale: The same fall means something quite different at 82.

questions.stem: Where do the numerical thresholds for significant mechanism come from?

options.text: A single national standard used everywhere
options.rationale: They vary between systems.

options.text: Local trauma triage criteria, which vary and are revised
options.rationale: Correct. Use your own service's figures, not a half-remembered number.

options.text: The patient's insurance provider
options.rationale: Not a clinical source.

options.text: The attending EMT's judgement alone
options.rationale: Judgement applies, but the criteria are written down locally.

questions.stem: A patient in a serious crash says they feel completely fine. How does this affect your index of suspicion?

options.text: It lowers it substantially
options.rationale: Adrenaline masks pain and distracting injuries hide others.

options.text: It does not lower it
options.rationale: Correct. Believe the mechanism over the reassurance.

options.text: It removes the need for a full assessment
options.rationale: The opposite is true.

options.text: It means the mechanism was overestimated
options.rationale: The mechanism is assessed from the scene, not the patient's mood.

questions.stem: Why do children warrant particular caution in trauma?

options.text: They cannot report symptoms at any age
options.rationale: Many can report symptoms perfectly well.

options.text: Energy is distributed through less body mass, organs sit closer, and they compensate then crash suddenly
options.rationale: Correct. Their compensation is what hides the severity.

options.text: They always have less serious injuries
options.rationale: They frequently have more serious ones.

options.text: They have greater physiological reserve so are never at risk
options.rationale: Their compensation masks injury, which is the danger.

questions.stem: What does a high index of suspicion change about your care?

options.text: Nothing; it is a theoretical concept
options.rationale: It changes three practical things.

options.text: Assessment thoroughness, transport timing, and what you say at handover
options.rationale: Correct. Saying the mechanism out loud changes how you are met.

options.text: Only the documentation
options.rationale: It changes clinical decisions as well.

options.text: Only whether you request air transport
options.rationale: That is one possible consequence among several.

questions.stem: Which trauma triage tier is assessed first?

options.text: Mechanism of injury
options.rationale: Mechanism is the third tier.

options.text: Physiological findings — vital signs and level of consciousness
options.rationale: Correct. Being abnormal now outranks every theory about mechanism.

options.text: Special considerations such as age
options.rationale: That tier is fourth.

options.text: Anatomical injuries
options.rationale: Anatomical criteria are second.

questions.stem: Why are trauma triage criteria deliberately over-inclusive?

options.text: To increase trauma centre funding
options.rationale: Not the rationale.

options.text: Because under-triage causes more harm than over-triage
options.rationale: Correct. The two errors are not equivalent.

options.text: Because EMTs cannot assess patients accurately
options.rationale: Not the reason.

options.text: To reduce the number of transports
options.rationale: They increase trauma centre transports, not reduce them.

questions.stem: A patient with normal vital signs has an open femur fracture. The local hospital is 6 minutes away; the trauma centre is 20. Where should they go?

options.text: The local hospital, since it is closest
options.rationale: Nearest is not automatically right when definitive care is elsewhere.

options.text: The trauma centre — the named injury meets anatomical criteria
options.rationale: Correct. Fourteen extra minutes beats an hour of transfer.

options.text: Whichever the patient prefers
options.rationale: Destination is a protocol decision, not a preference.

options.text: The local hospital, since the vital signs are normal
options.rationale: Anatomical criteria apply regardless of normal physiology.

options.rationale: Correct. It is the tier most often skipped.

options.text: Only the mechanism tier, reassessed
options.rationale: The mechanism tier has already been checked.

options.text: A refusal should be encouraged

questions.stem: How should the traditional one-hour figure be understood?

options.text: As a precise biological deadline
options.rationale: Nobody becomes unsalvageable at sixty-one minutes.

options.text: As a teaching construct — time matters continuously, without a threshold
options.rationale: Correct. Less time is better, with no cliff edge.

options.text: As a legal requirement for transport times
options.rationale: It is not a legal standard.

options.text: As applying equally to all patients
